newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portuguese to recreate first S.Atlantic flight.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese to recreate first S.Atlantic flight.

text.p: Almost 75 years after two Portuguese navy pilots braved the elements and flew across the south Atlantic for the first time, two air force pilots said on Wednesday they planned to repeat the journey in a replica plane.

The two captains, Jorge Santos and Joaquim Mestre, told a news conference they aimed to recreate the 63-hour crossing from Lisbon to Rio de Janeiro in a replica of the biplane that made the first trip between March and June 1922.
"We want to commemorate the original flight by Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral because we feel it never got the attention it deserved," Captain Mestre told a news conference.
"We want to celebrate the courage that the two Portuguese aviators showed," he said, dressed in his dark blue uniform.

The pilots said they would make a 10-day crossing including stops on five islands in March and April 1998 after they secured enough sponsorship from Portuguese companies to finance the construction of two replica planes.
It was still too early to estimate how much the enterprise would cost, the pilots said.
An English specialist company would build the planes, using the same wood and materials for the body as on the original plane, Santos said. One plane would be used as a reserve.
The engine and radio communications will be modern.
"It will still be a risky enterprise, but not nearly as dangerous as the original flight," Santos said.
The fragile plane, susceptible to strong winds, will fly at 80 knots (150 km) per hour.

Coutinho and Cabral risked their lives against bad weather and mechanical problems, showing remarkable flying and navigational skills as they hopped from island to island across 8,000 km (5,000 miles).
"We want people to understand their achievement in navigation," Mestre told Reuters.

Apart from a far superior engine, the two air force pilots will have another advantage over Coutinho and Cabral -- they will have accurate weather forecasts, which will allow them to steer clear of storms.
Once the journey is over, the two planes will be used for tourist flights over the River Tagus in Lisbon, Santos said.
